_about: The spec of kitcut.ai's template 'The conference in numbers' (studio/templates.py make --spec): what it is, what the film keeps of its sample (keep, generic), when the sample is the person's own event (identity), and its author's notes to Claude. Its film is projects/conference-numbers (local: the code is ours, the sample's logo is Web Summit's). caps: space -- the film's calendar page and its whip pan use sketch/space.js; it cuts no people out. generic: the template's own words for any event (stat labels, the months, common track names), so a remake that shares them is not stopped as a leftover.
title: The conference in numbers
description: An 88-second film that tells why to come to a conference in its own numbers -- as hype before the event or a recap after it: the logo assembles out of digits, a calendar marks the dates, a pin drops on the city, then each number rolls up like an odometer over a picture of what it counts (a crowd of dots, arcs flying in from the world, a city of blocks, a network, a wall of speakers, a clock, a timeline, camera flashes), the topics as a wall of words, a quote and the poster. Music only, no narration.
author: KitCut
example: Slush 2025 in numbers, as a recap -- slush.org
brief:
An 88-second film with no narration on a 120 bpm clock (a bar is 2 s): the logo assembles out of digits (they lock on the first hit, turn to pixels, then to the logo itself) with the headline and tagline under it and a ticker of the numbers along the foot; a calendar page swings down and marks the event's days; a pin drops on a dot map of the world at the venue; one chapter per number (they share 16-64 s); the topics as a wall of words; an optional quote; the poster. It works as hype before an event (last edition's numbers, the poster selling the next) or as a recap after it -- the headline says which year the numbers are from.

content.json is the whole job; film.js should rarely need a change.
- event: name; year (the edition the poster sells); numbers_year (the year the numbers are from: the headline is copy.headline, '{numbers_year} IN NUMBERS'); city; country; dates (short: 'NOV 9–12', <= 14 characters); dates_long; start and end as YYYY-MM-DD (they draw the calendar -- its month, the marked days, the 'N DAYS' count; without them the calendar is left out); month (the start month's name, in the film's language); venue (<= 30 characters reads best); lat and lon of the venue (the pin and the world map turn on them -- look them up); url (<= 24 characters); cta (<= 18); tagline (one line, <= 50).
- stats: 3 to 7, in the order they play; 5-7 is best (with 3, each chapter holds 16 s). Each: value written as the event writes it ('71,386', '1,2', '140' -- the digits roll, other characters stay), optional prefix ('€') and suffix ('+', 'M') in the accent colour, label (<= 24 characters; it may take two lines), optional note (one line, <= 40: a detail from the same source), and kind, which picks the picture: people (attendees, visitors: a crowd of dots), countries (arcs fly in from content.origins, [lat, lon] pairs, else from world hubs), companies (startups, exhibitors, partners: a city of blocks), network (investors, meetings, deals), speakers (a wall of tiles; images: [keys] puts faces or logos on them), sessions (talks, hours, tracks, workshops: a clock), years (editions: a timeline, a tick a year up to 60, with from/to labels), media (press, views, reach: camera flashes), type (anything else: the number alone, giant). Use each picture once where you can. The first three stats recap on the poster (or those marked poster: true).
- Never invent, round up or estimate a number: each must be on the event's own pages or its own press release, and all of them from the same year the headline names. If the event has published fewer than three, use what there is and say so.
- topics: 5-17 short track or theme names (<= 22 characters each), as the event names them; topics_title is the line above the wall (the event's own phrase if it has one, else copy.topics). quote (optional): a short press or attendee quote the event itself shows (<= 90 characters) with its source in by; without one the wall holds until the poster.
- palette: ground (the dark one), accent, second -- from the logo; every other shade is worked out. logo: {image, light} from template_pictures; without a logo the name, set in type, stands in, the opening's mosaic too.
- copy: the film's own words -- translate all of it for another language (weekdays start on Monday). The faces carry Latin and Cyrillic.
Tight places: the poster's dates and city lines and the calendar's left column fit about 12-16 characters at full size; the opening headline one line. Nothing is ever cut off -- it gets smaller -- so prefer short forms ('NOV 9–12', not 'NOVEMBER 9 TO 12'). The clock never changes with the content.
